nodes.label: Alice (editor)
nodes.summary: Applies her edit locally at once, then sends it. Keeps at most one operation in flight plus a buffer of later local edits.
nodes.details: This is the ot.js client protocol (Jupiter-style): states Synchronized, AwaitingConfirm, AwaitingWithBuffer. Google's 2010 post describes the same client-server idea. Read in an earlier pass.

nodes.label: Bob (editor)
nodes.summary: Receives Alice's operation, transforms it against any of his own unacknowledged edits, then applies it.

nodes.label: Connection gateway
nodes.summary: Long-lived WebSocket connections that carry operations and cursor/presence messages.
nodes.details: Figma, a different product, uses WebSockets to a server cluster with a separate process per document.

nodes.label: OT server (per document)
nodes.summary: Single authority per document: assigns each operation the next revision number, transforms it against operations the client had not seen, appends it to the log and broadcasts to every client.
nodes.details: A central server that assigns a total order is what lets client-server OT stay simple. The 2010 post describes replaying the log from the beginning (earlier pass).

nodes.label: Revision log
nodes.summary: Append-only list of transformed operations. The document is the replay of this log. Snapshots to shorten replay are an assumed optimisation.

nodes.label: Presence / cursors
nodes.summary: Broadcasts cursor positions and selections, transformed against concurrent edits.

nodes.label: Alternative: differential sync
nodes.summary: Fraser's algorithm: a symmetric loop of diff and fuzzy patch with shadow copies. Conflicts resolve automatically, but a patch whose context changed too much fails and is dropped.
nodes.details: Rejected for intent-sensitive editing because diffs carry no intent.

nodes.label: Alternative: CRDT
nodes.summary: Yjs/Automerge-style data types that converge without a central server. Figma is CRDT-inspired but keeps a central authority and last-writer-wins per property.
nodes.details: Some published algorithms show interleaving anomalies on concurrent inserts at the same spot (Kleppmann et al.).

nodes.label: Document server
nodes.summary: The per-document authority: the OT server, the revision log and presence.
nodes.details: Grouping container: it names the units the sources describe together. The components inside it are listed in the Components view.

steps.caption: Alice's editor applies the change to her screen immediately and sends the operation with the revision it was based on.
The connection gateway forwards it to the document's server.
The server transforms it against any operations it has applied since that revision, then assigns the next revision and appends it to the log.
It broadcasts the transformed operation to every client.
Bob's editor transforms it against his own pending edits and applies it. Alice receives it as an acknowledgement.

flows.name: Two people edit the same spot

steps.caption: Alice inserts text at position 3, based on revision 7.
Bob also inserted at position 3 based on revision 7. The server received his first, so it is revision 8.
The server transforms Alice's operation against Bob's: her insert shifts to account for his text, then becomes revision 9. Both intents survive and everyone converges to the same text.
Each client applies the operations it had not yet seen, transformed against its own pending edits.
The document is the replay of its revision log. (Snapshots are a common optimisation, but we do not claim Google uses them.)
Cursors and selections are broadcast and transformed against concurrent edits too.

flows.name: Alice loses her connection and returns

steps.caption: Alice reconnects with the last revision she saw (standard client behaviour).
The gateway hands her to the document's server.
The server reads the revision log after her last revision.
It sends the missing operations, which her client transforms against any local edits.
